body: Hungary uses long white standard European licence plates. Taxi licence plates are yellow, and newer electric vehicles have green plates. A newer format introduced in 2022 contains the coat of arms.

Hungarian bollards are black-and-white and wedge-shaped. They typically have a red reflector at the front and a white reflector at the back, though blue reflectors are also common. They are similar to Croatian bollards but appear less thin.

The most common utility pole is a concrete holey pole with thin holes going all the way to the ground. These can be distinguished from Polish poles (which don't have holes near the ground) and Romanian poles (which have wider or taller holes).
Hungarian chevrons are typically white on red. Less common are black-and-white chevrons.
The Hungarian language is unique for its many acute accents, umlauts on 'o's, and long words. The letters Ő and Ű, with double acute accents, are exclusive to Hungarian.
Hungarian street names commonly end with ‘utca’ or ‘út’, which are Hungarian words for 'street' and 'road' respectively.
Green kilometre markers can be seen along most Hungarian roads.
Hungarian sign posts are often abnormally tall, frequently appearing taller than the Street View camera.
Hungarian signs are typically attached with four bolts in a tall rectangular pattern, a feature not common in other Eastern European countries.
The most common pedestrian sign has five stripes and shows a person wearing a belt positioned noticeably low on the body. This 'sagging' appearance is unique to Hungary.
Hungarian numbered roads are marked with either green signs or, for 'M' highways, blue signs. The road numbers are displayed within a small shield shape.
Most directional signs are green with a white inner border and a green outer border. Signs on 'M' highways are blue with a similar border style.
A small, grey flag can sometimes be seen on the antenna of Generation 3 Google cars in Hungary, a feature shared with some neighbouring countries.
Much of the Generation 3 coverage in Hungary was taken during winter, giving it a grey and desolate appearance.
Hungarian houses are typically light-colored stone buildings with red tiled roofs. Suburban houses are often single-storey, while central ones can be taller and older but well-maintained.
While regular road lines are white, markings for bicycle lanes are typically yellow.
Hungarian area codes are two digits long, found at the beginning of 8-digit numbers or as the third and fourth digits of 10-digit numbers. Budapest has a unique area code of 1.
The first digit of Hungarian numbered roads follows a circular pattern centered around Budapest, making region-guessing easier.
Many Hungarian town names use local prefixes which can be very helpful for region-guessing.
Street signs with a thick metal frame are a strong indicator for the western part of Hungary.
Blue or green arrow-shaped street signs attached to utility poles are a strong clue for the county of Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg in the east.
The southeast of Hungary is extremely flat, while the north and west consist of forested hills and mountains. The tallest mountains are found in the north.
Lake Balaton is the only large lake in Hungary with Street View. The surrounding area is a hilly, built-up tourist destination with many small hotels.
The Puszta, centered around Hortobágy National Park, is a large area of natural, barren, and wet grasslands, unlike the cultivated plains elsewhere.
Many of Hungary's largest towns and cities have unique street signs that can be used for identification.
The road east of Tornanadaska, near the Slovakian border, is recognizable by the presence of snow, bollards, and an adjacent railway.
